summary: Marks the fiftieth anniversary of the RFC Series. It includes reflections from people involved at key points, a review of where the Series stands, and thoughts on its next fifty years. It updates the perspectives in RFC 2555 and RFC 5540.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8700 marks fifty years of the RFC Series with personal accounts from five people who shaped how it was run, a list of the moments that changed it, and a look at what is still unsettled: how the archive is preserved, what format RFCs are published in, and whether the Series is still separate from the IETF.

questions: when was the first rfc published
subtitle: How the RFC Series began, how it was run, and the questions its editors ask about its next fifty years.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series had no formal process for its first decades, and by 2019 it had grown to more than 8500 documents across four publication streams, leaving the editors to explain how it got there and where it should go.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects retrospective accounts from Steve Crocker on the origins, Vint Cerf on the editing team, Leslie Daigle on formalizing the RFC Editor model, Nevil Brownlee on the Independent stream and Sandy Ginoza on working inside the editor.
tldr.outcome: The document updates the perspectives in RFC 2555 and RFC 5540, and ends with three open questions for the next fifty years: digital preservation, the RFC file format, and whether the RFC Series and the IETF should remain distinct.

today: RFC 8700 is an Informational document from December 2019 that updates RFC 2555 and RFC 5540, the earlier anniversary accounts. No RFC obsoletes it, so it stands as the fiftieth-anniversary record of the Series, with the questions it raises about the next fifty years still open in the text.

sections.title: What the Series Is For
sections.content:
The RFC Series began in April 1969 with the publication of "Host Software" by Steve Crocker. The early RFCs were in fact requests for comments on ideas and proposals; the goal was to start conversations rather than to create an archival record of a standard or best practice. That goal changed over time as the formality of the publication process evolved and the community consuming the material grew. Today, over 8500 RFCs have been published, ranging across best practice guidance, experimental protocols, informational material and Internet standards.

Material is accepted for publication through the IETF, the IAB, the IRTF and the Independent Submissions streams, each of which has clear processes for how drafts are submitted and approved for publication as an RFC. The goal of the Series is to provide a canonical source for the material published by the RFC Editor and to support the preservation of that material in perpetuity.

The role of RFC Editor came a few years after the first RFC. The date the term was first used is unknown, but it was formalized by RFC 902 in July 1984; Jon Postel, the first RFC Editor, defined the role by his actions and later by defining the initial processes around publication. What is certain is that the goal of the RFC Editor is to produce documents that are readable, clear, consistent and reasonably uniform, and that the archival record of what has been published is maintained.

Change comes to the Series, albeit slowly. The distribution method changed from postal mail to FTP and then to email; some early RFCs were not even created electronically, but were written out by hand or on a typewriter. The process for creating RFCs became more structured, the editorial effort went from Steve Crocker to a designated editor, Jon Postel, and later to a team of five to seven individuals, and the editing and publishing work split from the service for registration of protocol code points. The structure was reviewed in RFC 4844, refined in RFC 5620 and refined again in RFC 6635, and in recent years the process to change the format of the RFC documents themselves has started under RFC 7990.

The RFC states that this is evolution, and that the Series will continue to be adapted to meet the needs of implementers, operators, historians and the community of authors that uses it, always balanced against the core mission of maintaining a strong, stable, archival record of technical specifications and other information relevant to the ARPANET and Internet networking communities.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs started as notes between colleagues asking each other what to think. Over time they became the permanent record of how the Internet works, and the people who publish them took on more structure, more review and more rules. This RFC describes that path from the inside.

sections.title: Key Moments and How Fast the Series Grew
sections.content:
The RFC lists a table of key moments in the history of the Series, running from the first RFC in April 1969 and the first distribution of RFCs over the network in April 1971, through the FYI, STD and BCP sub-series, the formalization of the document streams, and the move to a four-part RFC Editor organization in 2009, to the end of printing RFCs on paper in 2017.

The second table gives the average number of publications per year over five-year periods. The rate was 80 a year from 1969 to 1972, fell to 55 and then to 20 in the following two periods, and then rose steadily: 39, 69, 171, 237 and 325. The most recent two periods, 2008 to 2012 and 2013 to 2017, recorded 333 and 295. There were significant jumps in the publication rates in the 1990s and onward, with the number of publications almost doubling between 1993 and 2007. The annual submission count passed the 300 mark for the first time in 2004 and reached an all-time high of 385 in 2011, and it did not drop below 300 until 2016, when it was 284.

As the submissions grew, the RFC Editor experienced growing pains: processing times began to increase as the existing staff could not keep up with the growing queue. ISI brought on temporary copy editors to reduce the training hump and avoid permanently hiring staff in case the burst was a fluke. The effects of that experiment were lasting, because it led to the process used now, in which the RFC Editor asks more questions during AUTH and AUTH48 and technical changes require approval from the relevant Area Directors or stream managers. These changes added to the workload and extended publication times, and many now jokingly refer to AUTH48 as the authors' "48 days" or "48 weeks".
sections.plainLanguage: The number of RFCs published each year went from a few dozen in the early years to more than 300 a year in the 2000s. The editor's office grew to keep up, and the review step became more demanding in the process, so publication now takes longer than it once did.

sections.title: The Origins, by Steve Crocker
sections.content:
Steve Crocker recalls that the ARPANET procurement was initiated in the summer of 1968, with a Request for Quotations calling for four packet-switching devices, called Interface Message Processors, delivered to four sites in the western United States: UCLA, SRI International in Menlo Park, UCSB and the University of Utah. These sites ran different machines with different operating systems, and even details like character sets and byte sizes varied.

A meeting was called in August 1968 with representatives of the sites, chaired by Elmer Shapiro from SRI. The group, calling itself the Network Working Group, met at each of the sites over the following months, which set the precedent for regular face-to-face meetings. They took on the task of writing down their discussions, and Crocker organized the notes and assigned them numbers. The only rule he imposed was that a note had to be complete before he assigned a number, because he wanted to minimize holes in the sequence. He labelled the notes "Request for Comments" on Bill Duvall's suggestion, and the basic ground rules were that anyone could say anything and that nothing was official.

The notes were distributed by each institution sending a copy directly to each of the other participating institutions, with SRI's Network Information Center maintaining a central repository of everything. The RFCs were open in two important respects: anyone could write one for free and anyone could get them for free. In RFC 3, Crocker set the bar as low as possible, allowing any thought or suggestion, encouraging notes to be timely rather than polished, and setting the minimum length of a note at one sentence. Making the RFCs informal was not only a way of encouraging participation; it was important in making the communication effective, because one early participant had trouble writing an RFC when his institution wanted to subject them to publication review.

The group settled on a virtual bit stream layer as the basic building block for the protocols, because the essence of the network was peer-to-peer cooperation among machines and the processes inside them rather than a central machine controlling dependent devices. A virtual bit stream rather than a virtual byte stream was chosen because each computer had its own notion of how many bits were in a byte; 8-bit bytes did not become standard until a few years later. Jon Postel took over the care and feeding of the RFCs in 1971, evolving the process and adding collaborators over the next twenty-seven years.
sections.plainLanguage: The first RFCs were working notes from a small group of people designing the ARPANET. There was no standard to meet and no authority, so each note was a request for comments. They were numbered as they were written and passed from site to site by post, which is why the series is called what it is.

sections.title: Formalizing the Editor Model, by Leslie Daigle
sections.content:
Leslie Daigle, who chaired the Internet Architecture Board at a turning point in the institutions, describes how the IETF, IANA and the RFC Editor grew apart and then were re-formed. The IANA function was absorbed into a purpose-built international not-for-profit organization, the IETF created the IETF Administrative Support Activity and turned the Secretariat into one of its contracted functions, and the RFC Editor function was left as an independent effort supported by the Internet Society.

That independence was necessary for the historic role of the Series in considering all technical contributions, but it needed a governance and funding model of its own. There was also a risk that the Series would be perceived as the IETF's publication series, since the funding came from the Internet Society in the guise of support for the IETF, even though the Series predates the IETF by eighteen years and has historically carried documents that did not originate there. Daigle describes the tension around the idea of "push to publish", in which an RFC could be published by pressing a button once the IESG approved it. That would have reduced costs and improved timeliness, and avoided the specification issues introduced by copy editors hired as occasional workers, but it would not have kept the many significant text improvements those copy editors made, and not all RFCs are approved by the IESG.

The resolution was to place the governance of the RFC Editor function within reach of the Internet technical community rather than tying it to a particular private organization, under the oversight of the IAB, which is itself independent of the IETF. The IETF published requirements for its own technical publication service as RFC 4714. Daigle and the IAB then worked with the parties involved to produce RFC 4844, which captured the Series' mission as being for a purpose greater than IETF technical specification publication, and the roles and responsibilities of the parties involved. The RFC Editor is responsible for implementing that mission, the IAB keeps oversight responsibilities including policy oversight, and operational oversight migrated to the IETF Administrative Support Activity.
sections.plainLanguage: As the IETF grew and needed its own secretariat and its own publication process, the question arose of who owns the RFC Series. The answer settled on was to keep the Series separate from the IETF, but under the oversight of the Internet Architecture Board, so that anyone, not only the IETF, can publish into it.

sections.title: The Independent Stream and the Work of the Editor
sections.content:
Nevil Brownlee, Independent Submissions Editor from February 2010 to February 2018, describes how the Independent Stream works. All RFCs reach the Production Center as Internet-Drafts; they are copy edited until the edited version can be approved by their authors, which is the AUTH48 step, and at any stage authors can check their draft's status on the RFC Editor website. Once a draft has been reviewed and revised in dialogue with its reviewers, the Independent Submissions Editor submits it to the IESG for an IESG Review. A few drafts were controversial, and for those the editor worked with the IESG to negotiate an IESG Statement or an ISE Statement making clear why the editor published the draft.

One special part of the stream is the April 1st RFCs, which are humorous documents with no formal review and approval process. Authors must send them directly to the Independent Submissions Editor or the RFC Editor, only a few can be published each year, and each is reviewed by the ISE and the RFC Series Editor. Bob Braden's criteria were that they must relate to the Internet, their readers should reach the end of page two before realizing it is an April 1st RFC, and they must actually be funny. Brownlee published 159 RFCs in the Independent Stream during his eight years as editor.

Sandy Ginoza describes what the editor was like from the inside. When he joined ISI shortly after Jon Postel died, the RFC Editor functioned as one unit of four people. Bob Braden provided high-level guidance and reviewed Independent Submissions; Joyce Reynolds was a full-time employee who also served as a User Services Area Director and was on loan to IANA for half her time while IANA was being established; a part-time student programmer handled programming tasks, including parsing MIBs. Ginoza's own tasks were to manage the publication queue, format and prepare documents for Joyce's review, carry out AUTH48, and publish, index and archive the RFCs.

The infrastructure was upgraded as the load grew: the manual binder used to track RFC number assignment, a hand-edited HTML file for the queue page and a set of scripts that produced queue statistics were all replaced, an errata system was proposed and implemented, and XML became a newly accepted source file. When RFC 5620 was published in 2009 it did not go into effect until 2010, when the RFC Editor project was disbanded and split into the RFC Series Editor, the Independent Submissions Editor, the RFC Production Center and the Publisher function, with the RFC Series Advisory Group created to give expert guidance to the RFC Series Editor. The Production Center and Publisher contracts were awarded to Association Management Solutions in 2010.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every RFC comes from a working group. The Independent stream takes documents from anyone, and its editor arranges review, checks the copy editing and then submits the result for a second review before publication. The humorous April 1st documents have their own rules, including that the joke should not be obvious before the end of page two.

sections.title: The Next Fifty Years
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the Series began with goals of communication over formality and openness over structure, and that as the Internet has grown into a global construct the aim is still openness and communication, but for protocols and other information to support interoperability there must be points of stability to build from. Anyone, from small-time application developers to very large companies, is on the same footing, and anyone should be able to look back at a point in time and understand what was done and why.

Three topics are set out for the next fifty years. On preservation, the RFC Editor exists to edit, publish and maintain an archive, and a proper digital archive is more than saving RFCs to disk and backing up the disks. The document on digital preservation considerations for the RFC Series reviews what a digital archive means today, describes ways to support the archive into the future, and recommends ways for the RFC Editor to work with organizations that specialize in the field. The future will mean both finding new partners that can absorb and archive RFCs into a public, maintained digital archive, and reviewing the RFC format to make sure the published documents are archivable according to whatever the industry best practice is over time.

On the format, RFCs have been digital documents since very early in the Series, and while not always published in US-ASCII, that format has been the canonical format for decades, which the RFC calls remarkable. It does not extend far enough to meet the expectations of many users today, and a concerted effort started in 2012 to bring the Series into alignment with a new array of possibilities for preservation and display, with the initial reasoning and requirements recorded in RFC 7990.

On stream structure, the Series predates the IETF by eighteen years, but the IETF has become the source of the majority of documents submitted, policies developed for IETF stream drafts tend to apply across all four streams, and it is difficult for people to see how, or why, there is a distinction between the Series and the IETF. The RFC asks whether that distinction is artificial and should be removed, and notes that this is ultimately something the community will decide, with conversations underway on the ramifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are unsettled. How the archive of every RFC ever published is kept safe for the long term. What format RFCs are published in, since plain ASCII no longer fits what people expect from documents. And whether the RFC Series should be treated as one thing with the IETF rather than two, given that most documents come from the IETF anyway.

data.title: Documentation conventions
data.code:
The content of a NWG note may be any thought, suggestion, etc.
related to the HOST software or other aspect of the network.
Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished.
Philosophical positions without examples or other specifics,
specific suggestions or implementation techniques without
introductory or background explication, and explicit questions
without any attempted answers are all acceptable.  The minimum
length for a NWG note is one sentence.
